The Geometry of Scope
       Context, Visibility, and Translation Across Formal Systems

                               Flyxion
                             Independent Researcher

                           October 2026


                               Abstract
Formal languages, operating systems, computational environments, and interactive virtual
worlds employ different mechanisms for organizing context, visibility, and permissible
operations. Despite their differences, many admit representations in terms of nested or
overlapping domains, locally available information, transition relations, and structure-
preserving mappings.  This essay develops a mathematical framework for comparing
such systems without presupposing their equivalence. The primitive construction is a
contextual representation system, consisting of a small category of contexts, a set of
underlying states, a presheaf of context-indexed observations coherent with the restriction
arrows, an assignment of admissible actions, and a partial transition function. Knowledge,
presentation, and authority are shown to be independent assignments, so that hierarchical
containment alone forces no monotonicity of visibility or permission, and navigation
between contexts is separated from disclosure within a context by an explicit commutation
criterion. Filesystems, shell environments, lexical scope, access control, and game worlds
are treated as instances, and the orientation of information flow is identified as the
structural feature that distinguishes sections over regions from environments built by
accumulation. For every system, a canonical presheaf of observational distinctions is
constructed and characterized by a universal property, the coarsest quotient of the state
space compatible with a chosen family of contexts is characterized in the same way, and
the terminal system observed through a fixed observation presheaf is identified with its
global sections. Failures of local-to-global reconstruction are classified and exhibited by
finite examples. Translations between systems are then analyzed by what they preserve,
reflect, collapse, or invent: observational distinctions are preserved by every translation
and reflected exactly under an injectivity condition, authority is preserved only in a lax
direction that discards prohibitions, and surjectivity on states yields a common abstraction
without yielding equivalence. A representation theorem for tree-shaped systems shows
that a filesystem and a lexical scope discipline arise from one decorated rooted tree
by dual product constructions. The essay closes by separating a common abstraction
from categorical equivalence, from translation of proof theories, and from computational
universality, and argues that equivalence of heterogeneous formal systems is always
equivalence relative to the structure that a chosen abstraction retains.

Part I
The Mathematics of Context

1  Introduction:  Representation and Structural Correspon-
   dence

Programs, filesystems, shells, access-control policies, and the interactive worlds of video games
share a recurring design problem. At any moment a participant occupies some context, and
the context determines what can be seen, what can be named, what can be done, and where
one can go next. A block of source code determines which identifiers resolve and to what.
A directory determines which entries are listed and which paths are interpreted relative
to it. A process determines an environment, a working directory, and a set of credentials.
A level, a menu, or a room in an interactive world determines which objects are present,
which controls are live, and which exits are open. The recurrence is striking enough to invite
sweeping formulations, in which all of these are said to be trees, or hierarchies, or instances of
a single structure, and in which the further step is sometimes taken that all mathematical
languages are therefore equivalent. The purpose of this essay is to treat the recurrence as
a mathematical question while declining the sweeping formulations, and to determine by

                                        3

definitions, theorems, and counterexamples how much common structure there is and what
each comparison discards.
   Four claims need to be kept apart. The first is that two systems exhibit analogous
organizational patterns, which is a report of resemblance and carries no mathematical content
until the resemblance is made precise. The second is that the two systems admit mappings
into a common abstract structure. The third is that those mappings preserve specified
mathematical properties, such as reachability among contexts, distinctions among states, or
restrictions on action. The fourth is that the systems are equivalent under a specified notion
of equivalence. Only the first two are available at the outset, and the second is weaker than it
appears, because every system maps to a one-point system in which nothing is distinguished
and nothing is forbidden, so that the existence of a common abstraction is trivial unless the
abstraction is required to retain something. The third and fourth claims require explicit
conditions and proofs, and the results below are organized around the conditions under which
each can be established and the counterexamples that show where each fails.
   The central research question is the following: under what conditions can heterogeneous
formal systems be represented by a shared structure of contexts, observations, and admissible
transformations? The answer developed here has a definite form. Relative to a specified
family of observable structures, distinct systems possess a canonical common abstraction,
namely a coarsest quotient of states that retains exactly the distinctions the family can detect,
characterized by a universal property rather than selected by convenience. The differences
between the systems are then characterized by what that abstraction necessarily forgets:
the multiplicity of microstates behind each observable profile, the dynamics, the authority
structure, and the orientation in which information flows between nested contexts. The thesis
is therefore neither that all such systems are equivalent nor that nothing can be said in
common, but that equivalence is always equivalence relative to a retained structure, and that
the retained structure can be named, constructed, and proved canonical.
   Three levels of claim are distinguished throughout, and each numbered result carries
its level. The first level consists of established results from category theory, sheaf theory,
logic, and programming-language theory that serve as foundations; these are cited rather
than reproved, except where a short proof clarifies how a general fact applies to contextual
systems. The second level consists of results proved here, among them the commutation
criterion for navigation and disclosure, the canonical presheaf with its universal properties, the
terminal observed system, the relative equivalence theorem, the duality between regional and
accumulative information flow, the representation theorem for tree systems, the lax treatment
of authority, and the analysis of what is lost when a graph is replaced by a hierarchy. The
third level consists of conjectures and open questions, which are labeled as such. Appendix D
inventories every result with its status. No claim is made concerning human cognition; whether
people habitually employ these abstractions is an empirical question outside the scope of the
mathematics.
   The contribution is positioned as follows. The categorical ingredients are standard: the
canonical presheaf is an image factorization, the coarsest quotient is an intersection of kernels
with its universal property, and the terminal observed system is the limit of the observation

                                        4

presheaf, as the labels on Theorems 11.1, 11.3, and 13.4 record. What is proposed is a
unifying representation framework in which these ingredients are applied jointly to context,
observation, disclosure, authority, and transitions, together with comparative results that the
ingredients alone do not supply. Three of these are the center of the essay. First, regional
and accumulative information flow arise as dual product constructions on one decorated tree,
and the refinement categories they generate are isomorphic only when the tree is a chain
(Proposition 13.7). Second, observational equivalence and behavioral equivalence are kept
visibly apart: Example 13.6 exhibits two systems with one observational abstraction, differing
in a bounded counter, so that a translation exists in one direction and none exists in the other,
and the example is the model case of the distinction between what an abstraction retains and
what a stronger equivalence demands. Third, the representation theorem for tree systems
(Theorem 17.2) is stated for specified observational models over a common tree and makes
no claim of equivalence between filesystem and lexical-scope semantics. The framework is
compared with institutions and with scope graphs in Appendix E.
   The word context is used in at least two technical senses that must not be conflated. In the
theory of programs a context is a term with a hole, and two terms are contextually equivalent
when no context distinguishes their behavior [25]. Here a context is a position or region of
a system from which observations are made and operations are attempted, such as a scope,
a directory, a process, or a room. The two senses meet in Section 16, where quantification
over all program contexts is seen as quantification over a family of observation contexts in the
second sense.
   Part I (Sections 2 to 4) develops the mathematics of context: contexts as objects of
a preorder or category, the independence of knowledge, visibility, and authority, and the
separation of navigation from disclosure. Part II (Sections 5 to 8) examines four families of
examples: filesystems and shells, lexical scope, access control, and interactive worlds. Part III
(Sections 9 to 11) introduces the presheaf of observations, the local-to-global reconstruction
problem, and the quotient of states by observational equivalence. Part IV (Sections 12 to 16)
defines the category of contextual representation systems and studies translation, covering
common abstractions, the distinction among surjectivity, fullness, faithfulness, and equivalence,
translation among mathematical languages, and universality. Part V (Sections 17 to 20)
assembles the general construction and its representation theorems, analyzes preservation and
loss, examines the limits of hierarchical representation, and concludes.

2  Contexts as Mathematical Objects

Definition 2.1 (Context system). A context system is a triple C = (C, ⪯, T) in which C is
a set of contexts, ⪯⊆C × C is a relation of nesting, read c ⪯d as “c is nested in d”, and
T ⊆C × L × C is a set of labeled navigation transitions over a set L of labels.

   Nesting is naturally reflexive and transitive: every context lies within itself, and a context
within a context within a third lies within the third. Reflexivity and transitivity make ⪯
a preorder. Antisymmetry is a further demand that fails in practice whenever two distinct

                                        5

contexts are mutually nested, as happens when two names denote one directory through a bind
mount, or when a module is entered through two aliases. Retaining the preorder keeps both
names, while passing to the poset quotient identifies them, which is harmless for questions
about observations and harmful for questions about naming. The relation supplied by a
presentation is usually not transitive but is the generating relation of its reflexive transitive
closure, as with the parent-child edges of a directory tree, whose closure is the ancestor
relation. The distinction between a generating relation and the preorder it generates returns
in Section 19.
    Several shapes of nesting occur in practice and need to be distinguished. A nested hierarchy
is one in which each context has a single immediate container. A graph with multiple parents
arises from hard links, multiple inheritance, and shared modules. A graph with cycles arises
from mutually recursive modules and from portals in interactive worlds; in the reflexive
transitive closure a cycle collapses its vertices into one equivalence class, so a preorder cannot
distinguish a cycle from a set of aliases. Overlapping contexts, such as two windows or two
permission regions that intersect without either containing the other, are most naturally
modeled as subsets of a set of locations ordered by inclusion, with intersection as meet
whenever it exists, a point developed in Section 9. The hierarchical case admits a crisp
characterization.
Proposition 2.2 (Rooted trees as posets; established). A finite poset (C, ⪯) is a rooted
tree under the ancestor relation, with the root as greatest element, if and only if it has a
greatest element and, for every c ∈C, the set ↑c = {d : c ⪯d} is a chain.

Proof. In a rooted tree with c ⪯d meaning that d lies on the path from c to the root, ↑c is
that path, which is a chain, and the root is greatest. Conversely, given a greatest element ⊤
and chains ↑c, the set ↑c \ {c} is a finite chain, nonempty when  c̸ = ⊤because it contains
⊤, so it has a least element, which is declared the parent of c. The resulting parent function
defines a rooted tree whose ancestor relation is ⪯.

   The consequence used repeatedly is that in a rooted tree the ancestors of any node are
linearly ordered, so a node with two incomparable ancestors cannot occur in any tree.
Proposition 2.3 (Categories from contexts; established).   (a) A preorder (C, ⪯) is a thin
      category C⪯with a unique arrow c →d exactly when c ⪯d. Functors between such cate-
      gories are monotone maps, and the category is skeletal exactly when ⪯is antisymmetric.
  (b) A directed graph G generates a free category Path(G) whose arrows are finite directed
      paths, the empty path included, and a full functor Path(G) →Reach(G) onto the preorder
      of reachability, which is the identity on objects. This functor is faithful if and only if G
       is acyclic and has at most one directed path between any two vertices.

Proof. Part (a) is the standard identification of a preorder with a category in which composition
is transitivity and identities are reflexivity. For (b), Path(G) is full over Reach(G) because
every reachable pair is joined by some path. The functor is faithful exactly when each hom-set
of Path(G) has at most one element, which fails when two distinct paths join the same vertices,

                                        6

and fails at a vertex lying on a directed cycle, where the empty path and the cycle are distinct
arrows v →v.

   The distinction in part (b) between routes and reachability is the first instance of a pattern
that organizes the essay: a representation can retain the arrow or only the fact that an arrow
exists, and the two give different theories. A graph with vertices h, a, b, r and edges h →a,
h →b, a →r, b →r has two arrows h →r in Path(G) and one in Reach(G); whether a
system treats these as the same position depends on whether the route taken is part of the
state. Section 5 shows that the logical working directory of a shell retains the route and the
physical working directory retains only the endpoint.
   Two orders on the same set of contexts will be in play and must not be confused. The nesting
preorder ⪯records containment, while Section 9 introduces a refinement order recording
which context observes more. For a filesystem viewed through subtrees the two coincide, and
for lexical scope they are opposite, a fact whose consequences occupy Sections 13 and 17.

3  Scope, Visibility, and Authority

Fix a set I of informational items, such as bindings, directory entries, or facts about a world,
and a set Σ of operations. To each context c three subsets are assigned. The set K(c) ⊆I is
the information available to an observer located at c. The set V (c) ⊆K(c) is the information
exposed by a particular interface at c, subject to the design discipline that an interface
cannot present what is unavailable. The set A(c) ⊆Σ is the set of operations admissible at
c. Knowledge, presentation, and authority are independent in the precise sense that none
determines the others. A hidden file lies in K(c) but not V (c) until a disclosure is performed;
a read-only file lies in V (c) while the write operation on it lies outside A(c); an operation may
be admissible at a context whose interface no longer displays the object it acts upon. The
interesting question is how these assignments vary along the nesting relation, and the answer
is that nesting alone constrains none of them.

Proposition 3.1 (No forced monotonicity; proved here). Let c ≺d be strictly nested
contexts, and let I and Σ be sufficiently large sets of information items and actions. For
each of K, V , and A and for each of the relations strict inclusion, reverse strict inclusion,
equality, and incomparability, there exist assignments of subsets of I or Σ to c and d for
which the values at c and d stand in that relation. For V the assignments are required to
satisfy V (e) ⊆K(e) at each context e, so the relation between V (c) and V (d) is realizable for
each of the four relations but is not independent of the relation between K(c) and K(d); for
example, K(c) = ∅forces V (c) = ∅. Moreover, on a three-element chain c1 ≺c2 ≺c3, each
assignment can be neither monotone nor antitone.

Proof. For the first claim, choose subsets of I or Σ realizing the desired relation; for V ,
choose V (c) and V (d) among the subsets of K(c) and K(d) respectively, which is possible
for each relation because V = K and V = ∅are both permitted. For the second claim take
I = {1, 2, 3, 4}, Σ = {r, w, x}, and the following assignment.

                                        7

c1      c2       c3

                 K   {1, 2}  {1}    {1, 3}
                        V    {1}   {1}     {3}
                   A    {r}   {w}   {r, w, x}

Here K(c1) ⊋K(c2) ⊊K(c3), while V (c2) and V (c3) are incomparable and A(c1) and A(c2)
are incomparable. Hence none of the three assignments is monotone or antitone along the
chain, and V ⊆K holds throughout.

   The finite counterexample is not an artifact. Lexical scope makes the information available
to an inner block grow with depth, a sandbox or a changed root directory makes it shrink,
a setuid program or a privilege-granting command makes authority grow on entry, and
attenuation of a capability makes it shrink. Hierarchical context inclusion therefore entails no
monotonicity of visibility or authority, and any claim that deeper contexts see less, or can do
less, or see more, or can do more, is a property of a specific discipline rather than of nesting.
   The next definition fixes the primitive construction on which the remainder of the essay is
built. It follows a deliberate convention about the direction of arrows: an arrow u : c →d
means that c is a restriction of d, so that d is the observationally richer of the two. This
convention is chosen so that observations restrict along arrows in the manner of a presheaf,
and it is independent of the nesting order, which may agree with it or oppose it.

Definition 3.2 (Contextual representation system). A contextual representation system is a
quintuple
                   R = (C, X, Ω, A, δ)
together with an alphabet Σ of actions, consisting of the following.
  (1) A small category C of contexts. An arrow u  : c →d is a refinement arrow: c is a
      restriction of d.
  (2) A set X of underlying states.
  (3) A presheaf Ω: Cop →Set of observation spaces, with restriction maps Ω(u) : Ω(d) →
     Ω(c) for u : c →d, together with observation maps oc : X →Ω(c).
  (4) A context-indexed assignment of admissible actions A : Ob(C) →P(Σ).
  (5) A partial transition function δ : X × Σ ⇀X.
The observation maps must satisfy observation coherence: for every arrow u : c →d,

                                         oc = Ω(u) ◦od.

   Coherence is a modeling assumption, not a law of operating systems, and several real
disciplines violate it as stated; Section 9 shows that the flat visible environment of a language
with shadowing is one, and repairs it. The definition requires neither that authority nor that
action sets increase with observational richness. Movement of an observer from one context

                                        8

to another is not an arrow of C; it is a transition of the system, represented by δ over a state
space that records position, or by the explicit configuration spaces of Section 4. This keeps
the arrows of C for the single purpose of carrying the coherence of observations.

Theorem 3.3 (Observational refinement; proved here). For every context c let x ∼c y if
and only if oc(x) = oc(y). Then for every arrow u : c →d,

                              ∼d ⊆∼c.

Proof. If x ∼d y then od(x) = od(y), and applying Ω(u) and using coherence gives oc(x) =
Ω(u)od(x) = Ω(u)od(y) = oc(y).

   This is the first substantive consequence of the definition: richer observations distinguish
at least as many states as their restrictions. It is a statement about observation only, and it
carries no implication for authority.

Proposition 3.4 (Independence of authority; proved here). Observational refinement
implies neither A(c) ⊆A(d) nor A(d) ⊆A(c) for an arrow u : c →d.

Proof. Let C have two objects c, d and one non-identity arrow u : c →d. Let X = {0, 1},
Ω(d) = {0, 1}, Ω(c) = {∗}, with Ω(u) the constant map, od = id, and oc constant. Coherence
holds, and ∼d is the diagonal while ∼c identifies both states, consistent with Theorem 3.3. Let
Σ = {a, b} with A(c) = {a} and A(d) = {b}. The two action sets are disjoint and nonempty,
so neither inclusion holds.

    Proposition 3.4 separates visibility from permission formally, and Section 7 shows that the
order for which authority is monotone is a different order again, the order of delegation.

4  Navigation and Disclosure as Distinct Operators

An observer’s situation is a pair consisting of a position and a disclosure state, the latter
recording display options such as whether hidden entries are shown or whether filename
extensions are displayed. Let S be a set of disclosure states and let Conf = C × S be the set
of configurations. A navigation transition t = (c, ℓ, c′) ∈T induces a partial map

                    Nt : Conf ⇀Conf,      (c, s) 7→(c′, ρt(s)),

defined on {c} × S, where ρt : S →S records the policy by which display settings are carried
across the transition. A family f = (fc)c∈C of partial maps fc : S ⇀S induces a disclosure
operator
                  Df : Conf ⇀Conf,      (c, s) 7→(c, fc(s)),
which changes the disclosure state within the same context. Both are typed as partial maps on
Conf, so that the composites NtDf and DfNt are meaningful and the question of commutation
is well posed; without this typing the equation ND = DN is shorthand and nothing more.

                                        9

Proposition 4.1 (Commutation criterion; proved here). Let t = (c, ℓ, c′).  If all maps
involved are total on S, the composites NtDf and DfNt agree on {c} × S if and only if

                                      ρt ◦fc = fc′ ◦ρt  on S.

In particular:
   (i) if ρt = idS, navigation and disclosure commute exactly when fc = fc′;
  (ii) if ρt is constant with value s0, they commute exactly when fc′(s0) = s0;
 (iii) if fc is defined at s and fc′ is undefined at ρt(s), then NtDf is defined at (c, s) while
    DfNt is not, so the composites differ as partial maps.

Proof. Computing, NtDf(c, s) = (c′, ρt(fc(s))) and DfNt(c, s) = (c′, fc′(ρt(s))), which are
equal for all s exactly when the displayed identity holds. Case (i) substitutes ρt = id. Case
(ii) gives s0 = fc′(s0). Case (iii) is read off from the definitions of the composites as partial
maps.

   The identity ρtfc = fc′ρt is an intertwining condition, the statement that the policy ρt is
equivariant with respect to the disclosure operators on the two sides of the transition. Its
failure has everyday instances. In a file manager that stores a “show hidden entries” setting
per folder, S = {0, 1}C, ρt = id, and fc toggles the coordinate of c; then fc̸ = fc′ and the order
of toggling and navigating matters, since toggling and then navigating carries the toggled state
to the new folder’s configuration while navigating and then toggling acts on the new folder’s
own coordinate. When the setting is global, S = {0, 1} and fc is the same toggle everywhere,
and navigation and disclosure commute. When entering a folder resets the display to a default
s0 at which the toggle is not a fixed point, case (ii) shows that disclosure performed before
navigation is always lost, whereas disclosure performed after navigation is not. A virtual
folder with no notion of hidden entries realizes case (iii).
    Disclosure at a fixed context is governed by a refinement relation among observation maps,
which is the same structure as Theorem 3.3 at a single context.
Definition 4.2 (Disclosure refinement). At a fixed context c, let o(0)c    : X →Y0 and o(1)c    : X →
Y1 be two observation maps. Observation 1 refines observation 0 if there exists r : Y1 →Y0
with o(0)c = r ◦o(1)c   .
Theorem 4.3 (Disclosure refinement; proved here). If observation 1 refines observation 0
then ker(o(1)c  ) ⊆ker(o(0)c  ). The inclusion is strict exactly when the richer observation separates
at least one pair of states that the coarser one identifies.

Proof.  If o(1)c  (x) = o(1)c  (y) then applying r gives o(0)c  (x) = o(0)c  (y). Strictness is the statement
that the two kernels differ, which is the existence of a pair in ker(o(0)c  ) \ ker(o(1)c  ).

   This formalizes the difference between an ordinary directory listing and one that also
reveals dotfiles, and equally the difference between a listing that shows base names and one
that shows names with extensions: in each case the second observation determines the first

                                       10

by discarding detail, and the discarded detail is exactly what the strict inclusion of kernels
measures. Disclosure moves along refinement within a context, whereas navigation moves
between contexts, and Proposition 4.1 identifies when the two can be reordered.

Part II
Hierarchical and Computational
Representations

5  Filesystems and Shell Environments

A filesystem state can be modeled as a structure F = (N, Ndir, r, ent, mode) in which N is
a set of nodes, Ndir ⊆N the directories, r ∈Ndir the root, ent : Ndir × Names ⇀N the
directory-entry function, and mode : N →Modes an assignment of permission bits. Symbolic
links are nodes that carry a target path, and the entries . and .. are ordinary entries of
each directory, the latter naming the physical parent. Path resolution is the partial function
resF  : Ndir × Paths ⇀N obtained by iterating ent along the components of a path, expanding
symbolic links when they are met. In the special case where the graph of ent, omitting ., ..,
and links, is a rooted tree, the filesystem is a hierarchy in the sense of Proposition 2.2. Hard
links to files make the structure a directed acyclic graph in which a file has several parents, so
that the path to a file is no longer unique, and symbolic links add edges that need not respect
the tree at all.
   The working directory of a shell illustrates the difference between a route and an endpoint
recorded in Proposition 2.3. A POSIX shell maintains a logical working directory as a path
string, and the built-in that changes directory behaves differently under the logical option and
the physical option when symbolic links are present [32]. If link in /home/u is a symbolic
link to /var/data, then changing into link and then into ..  returns to /home/u under
logical resolution and moves to /var under physical resolution, because the physical parent of
/var/data is /var. The parent of a context is therefore not a function of the node alone once
links are present: the logical working directory retains an arrow of the path category, and the
physical working directory retains only a point of the reachability preorder. A correct model
of the context in which a relative path is interpreted must say which of the two the shell uses,
and the logical choice is the unfolding of the graph into paths that Section 19 analyzes.
  A process adds a second layer that is distinct from the filesystem. A process state includes
a working directory, an environment mapping variable names to strings, a file-creation mask,
credentials, and open file descriptors. The process tree is generated by spawning: a child
created by fork receives a copy of its parent’s state at the moment of creation, and a subshell
is such a child. Inheritance is therefore a snapshot and not a live reference, since later changes
to the parent’s environment do not reach an existing child and changes made by the child
vanish when it exits. This contrasts with a closure in a lexically scoped language, which


                                       11

captures the location of a binding and so remains coupled to later updates, as Section 6 shows.
A third layer is the command interpreter, whose resolution of a command name consults an
ordered list: aliases, then shell functions, then built-ins, then the directories named in the
search path in order, and the first match wins. This ordered list has the form of a scope chain,
but the order is fixed by the interpreter and not by nesting.
   Changing the working directory, entering a subshell, and altering file permissions share
contextual features, for each changes what some later operation will see, yet they are mathe-
matically distinct. To make this precise, let the configuration of the system be F × Proc+,
a filesystem state together with a nonempty tree of processes with one designated current
process. Let cdd change the working directory of the current process, defined when the process
holds search permission on d; let sub create a child copy of the current process and make it
current; let exit discard the current process and return to its parent; and let chmodd,m set the
mode of d to m, defined for the owner.
Proposition 5.1 (Distinctness of cd, sub, and chmod; proved here).   (a) The three oper-
     ations modify different components of the configuration F × Proc+: cdd changes only
      the working-directory coordinate of the designated process, sub changes only the process
      tree and the designation of the current process, and chmodd,m changes only the mode
      coordinate of F. Their domains of definition nevertheless read other components, since
      cdd consults the modes in F and the credentials of the current process, and chmodd,m
      consults the ownership recorded in F against those credentials.
  (b) They have different persistence. For every finite sequence w of environment-modifying
      operations and working-directory changes performed between sub and the matching exit,
      the composite exit ◦w ◦sub restores the parent’s coordinates to their former values,
     whereas cdd alters the working directory of the current process and chmodd,m alters the
     permissions seen by every process.
  (c) They do not commute. If an unprivileged process owns a directory d on which it holds
     search permission, then the sequence cdd followed by chmodd,000 is defined, while the

A program is parsed into an abstract syntax tree, and the binding forms of the language,

binding and not syntactic adjacency, and a more faithful structure is the scope graph [29].

whenever any such position exists, so the value selected is determined by (v, n).

to every language, since languages with dynamic evaluation of names or with ambiguous
imports may not supply a finite ordered sequence. Python is a useful test case because its

that distinguish the policy ϱ from simple traversal of ancestors [33]. At compile time every
name occurring in a function body is classified. A name that is bound anywhere in the body,
by assignment, import, definition, or loop variable, is local unless declared otherwise, and this
classification covers binding occurrences that follow the use. For a local name, ϱ(v, n) = (v),

does not continue outward. A name that is used but not bound locally is free, and its eligible

7  Access Control and Contextual Authority

The access-matrix model of protection associates to each pair of a principal and an object
a set of rights [19]. A capability is an unforgeable reference that carries rights and can be
passed from one holder to another [10]. Discretionary access control, as in the permission
bits of a Unix filesystem, attaches rights to objects and grants them according to the identity
and group of the requester. In a capability discipline there is no ambient authority, so that

                                       15

authority arises only from references actually held [7]. Execution environments inherit part of
their authority from their creators, but inheritance is mediated by explicit mechanisms such
as dropping privileges, changing identity on execution of a privileged program, and passing
descriptors.
   The natural question is whether authorization is a functorial assignment to contexts, that
is, whether a context-indexed set of admissible operations is monotone with respect to the
relevant order, so that A : (C, ≤) →(P(Σ), ⊆) is a functor. The answer depends entirely
on which order is meant, because three distinct orders are attached to the same execution
contexts. The first is containment, the nesting of directories or scopes. The second is spawn,
the process tree in which each process is created by another. The third is delegation, in
which c ⊑d when the authority of c is obtained by passing a subset of the authority of d.
Authority is monotone with respect to delegation by construction, and the content of the next
proposition is that it need not be monotone with respect to either of the others.

contexts, three orders on it for containment, spawn, and delegation, and an assignment A such
that A is monotone with respect to delegation and not monotone with respect to containment
or spawn. In particular authorization need not decrease with depth in a hierarchy.

Proof. Let the contexts be u, a user shell with working directory /home; l, a sandboxed child
with working directory /home/sandbox; and s, a program with elevated authority started by
u with working directory /home/bin. Containment gives l ⪯u and s ⪯u. Spawn gives l
and s as children of u. Delegation gives l ⊑u only, since s holds authority that u did not
pass to it. Let A(u) = {read, write}, A(l) = {read}, and A(s) = {read, write, admin}. Then
A(l) ⊆A(u), consistent with delegation, while s ⪯u and s is a child of u with A(s)̸ ⊆A(u),
so monotonicity fails for containment and for spawn.

name requires search permission on every directory along the path, so the right to reach
decreases, in the sense of a conjunction, along the path. After a file has been opened, however,
the descriptor is a capability, and later access is checked against the object and the descriptor’s
rights and not against the ancestors of the original path. The same object thus has authority
that is decreasing in depth for name resolution and independent of depth for held references.

safety problem for the general access-matrix model, which asks whether a right can leak to a
principal that lacks it [17]; Section 18 returns to what translations can and cannot preserve
about prohibitions.

An interactive environment is represented as a labeled transition system G = (S, Σ, −→) with

floor of a building. Logical nesting is a stack of modes, as of a menu opened over a level.

15  Translation Between Mathematical Languages

Set-theoretic, type-theoretic, logical, algebraic, and categorical presentations of mathematical
structure are connected by translations of different strengths, and the discussion above supplies
a vocabulary for keeping them apart. A syntactic translation from a theory T to a theory
T ′ is a compositional map ϕ 7→ϕ∗of formulas such that T ⊢ϕ implies T ′ ⊢ϕ∗, and it
reflects provability when the converse holds. A semantic interpretation is a functor between
categories of models, typically a reduct. Two theories are definitionally equivalent when they
have a common definitional extension, and Morita equivalent when, after adding new sorts for
products, subsorts, and quotients, they are definitionally equivalent [5]. Finally the categories
of models may be equivalent as categories. These notions are logically independent: a syntactic
translation need not reflect provability, a semantic interpretation need not be an equivalence,
and categorical equivalence of models need not come from any translation of syntax with
preserved proof theory. The following examples show each separation concretely.

16  Universality and Its Limits

Computational universality is a statement that a formalism computes every computable
function. The strongest form of the observation that universal systems are interchangeable
is Rogers’ isomorphism theorem: any two acceptable numberings of the partial computable
functions, which includes the programming systems of any two universal languages, are
related by a computable bijection of program indices that preserves the function computed
[36]. Universality therefore yields a translation between any two universal systems, and the
translation preserves exactly one thing, the input-output function of each program. In the
terminology above, it is a surjective representation onto a one-observation system, the weakly
terminal abstraction of Proposition 13.3 specialized to the observation “what function is
computed”. Nothing else need be preserved, and in general nothing else is.
   Several distinct kinds of structure are lost. Resource behavior depends on the model:
translating between Turing machines and random-access machines costs a polynomial overhead,
so complexity classes defined up to polynomial factors are stable, while fine-grained time
bounds are not, and whether the stability extends to every physically realizable model is open,
with quantum computation the principal candidate for violating it if the relevant complexity
classes differ. Expressive power in a language-design sense is finer than computability: one
language is more expressive than another when a construct cannot be eliminated by local
rewriting without global reorganization of programs [11]. Definability at higher types separates
languages that compute the same first-order functions: the parallel-or operator is not definable
in the language PCF, though it is computable, and adding it yields the language for which
the standard model is fully abstract [31]. Type systems and proof theories differ for languages
with the same computable functions, as the contrast between simply typed and untyped
lambda calculi illustrates.

let the family U of closing program contexts be a discrete set of observation contexts, and

19  The Limits of Hierarchical Representation

A tree is the most economical structure for nested contexts, supporting induction on structure,
a unique chain of ancestors, and canonical forms. Several features of the systems examined
here are not trees, and each one represents information that a hierarchy either discards or
must reintroduce by additional structure.

Overlapping scopes and multiple parents. A context with two incomparable containers,
as in the diamond of Proposition 6.5, has no unique chain of ancestors, so resolution needs
a policy that linearizes the containers. Python’s attribute lookup for classes uses the C3
linearization, so that for classes A, B(A), C(A), and D(B,C) the lookup order for D is D, B, C, A,
object [27]. The linearization is an additional datum, not a consequence of the poset, and it
can fail to exist: declaring a class with bases A and then B(A) in that order is rejected because
no linear order is consistent with the constraints. A hierarchy of classes underdetermines
resolution, and the underdetermination is resolved by structure the hierarchy does not contain.

Cycles.  Mutually dependent modules form a cycle in the import graph. The reflexive
transitive closure collapses a cycle to an equivalence class, which retains reachability and loses
the order of entry, yet the behavior of a cyclic import depends on which module is entered

first, since the second sees a partially initialized first. The behavior depends on the route and
not only on the reachability relation, which is the distinction of Proposition 2.3.

contexts in ways that do not respect any nesting, and the edge from one context to another
may exist only in some states, so that the unguarded context graph over-approximates by
Proposition 8.1.

run time or by procedural generation of levels, the set of contexts is a function of the state,
and a representation with a fixed small category C is not available. The remedy is to take

context currently exists, which moves the dynamics into the observation.

uniqueness of names or acyclicity of dependencies, is not expressible along the edges of a tree,

not been supplied here. In summary, a tree representation is useful without being structurally
complete: it preserves behavior up to bisimulation when state lives in the configuration, and
it loses identity of repeated contexts, finiteness in the presence of cycles, and the nonlocal
constraints that must be reintroduced as descent, guards, stacks, or linearizations.

20  Conclusion: Equivalence Relative to Abstraction

The central question was under what conditions heterogeneous formal systems can be repre-
sented by a shared structure of contexts, observations, and admissible transformations. The
development has given the question a determinate answer in four parts. First, a common
abstraction always exists in a trivial sense and is informative only relative to what it retains,
since there is a terminal system that retains nothing and a disjoint union that retains ev-
erything while identifying nothing (Proposition 13.3). Second, relative to a chosen family
of observations, a canonical abstraction exists and is characterized by universal properties:

                                       42

the canonical presheaf of observational distinctions is the coarsest presheaf quotient through
which observations factor (Theorem 11.1), the quotient of states by a family of contexts is
the coarsest compatible with the family (Theorem 11.3), and the set of global sections is
the terminal system observed through a fixed presheaf (Theorem 13.4). Third, translations
preserve observational distinctions always and reflect them exactly when the observation map
is injective on its image (Theorem 12.3 and Proposition 12.4), preserve permitted behavior
while discarding prohibitions (Proposition 18.2), and preserve reachability when bounded
(Proposition 18.1). Fourth, surjective and even faithful representations establish equivalence
only of the canonical presheaves (Theorem 14.6), and the examples show that this leaves
the dynamics, the authority structure, the multiplicity of microstates, and the orientation of
information flow free to differ (Example 13.6, Proposition 13.7).
   The difference between the existence of a common abstraction and the claim that all
mathematical languages are equivalent is therefore a difference of quantifiers over structure. A
common abstraction asserts that some structure is shared. Equivalence asserts that all relevant
structure is shared, and a theory of what is relevant is what a notion of equivalence supplies:
categorical equivalence of posets collapses to isomorphism (Proposition 14.4), equivalence of
presheaf categories does the same (Corollary 14.5), translation between logics may preserve
provability in one direction without reflecting it (Proposition 15.1), and computational
universality equates languages only at the level of the function computed (Section 16). The
statement that survives is the one with which the essay began: distinct mathematical languages
can possess a canonical common abstraction relative to a specified family of observable
structures, while their differences are characterized by the information and operations that
the abstraction necessarily forgets. The statement is not a theorem about all languages;
it is a method, and its range is the class of systems that can be presented as contextual
representation systems, which includes the filesystems, lexical scope disciplines, access-control
models, and transition systems treated here, and whose boundary is not yet known.
    Several directions follow. In categorical semantics, the category CRS and its observational
reduct Part invite a study of limits and colimits, beginning with Question 17.5, and of
an internal logic for contextual systems in which the sheaf condition and its failures are
logical notions. In contextual logic, the independence of knowledge, visibility, and authority
suggests a modal treatment in which the three assignments are separate modalities, and
the commutation criterion of Proposition 4.1 becomes an equation between modalities. In
programming-language theory, the observation that full abstraction is the canonical quotient
(Proposition 16.1) suggests comparing scope disciplines by the kernel families they induce, and
the representation theorem for trees (Theorem 17.2) suggests extending decorated trees to
scope graphs with the guards and linearizations of Section 19. In mathematical representation,
the relation of the present construction to frameworks for translation among logics, such as
institutions, is outlined in Appendix E and remains to be worked out, as do Question 15.3
and the relation to simulation-based accounts of reasoning in Question E.1. Throughout,
the results are stated with their hypotheses, and the conjectures are marked as such. The
strongest version of the claim that heterogeneous formal systems are one structure is not
supported by the mathematics, and the weaker versions are supported to exactly the degree

η : F ⇒G between functors F, G : C →D is a family ηc : Fc →Gc with ηdF(u) = G(u)ηc

E  Related Frameworks and Bibliographic Notes

The categorical background is standard [21, 6], with an accessible account in [4] and the
treatment of sheaves and sites in [22]. The programming-language background draws on
[15, 30], program analysis on [28], and the semantics of objects on [1]. The scope-graph
formulation of name resolution adopted in Section 6 is that of [29], and the use of presheaf-
valued observation relative to contexts follows the spirit of sheaf-theoretic treatments of
contextuality [2].  Action semantics [26] and categorical combinators [9] are alternative
frameworks for modular semantics of programming languages, and the groupoid interpretation
of type theory [16] is a categorical semantics in which identity is itself structured.  For
translation among logics, the theory of institutions [14] provides a general framework in which
a logical system is a functor from signatures to satisfaction relations and translations are
morphisms of such functors, and relating contextual representation systems to institutions
is a natural next step noted in Section 20. For access control, the original formulations are
[19, 10], the undecidability of safety is [17], and the object-capability discipline is discussed
in [7]. The suggested reading list from which the present development started is a list of
starting points for a literature review, and the inclusion of a work in it is not a claim that the
construction proposed here has been established there.

Comparison with institutions.  An institution assigns to each signature a category of
models and a set of sentences, with a satisfaction relation that is invariant under change of
signature [14]. Three features of the present framework are representable in that setting,
and three are not without extra structure. The observational kernel ∼c of a context is
the theory-indistinguishability relation of the models relative to a fixed set of sentences, so
the canonical presheaf Q corresponds to the quotient of models by elementary equivalence
relative to the sentences available at c, and the restriction maps correspond to signature
inclusions. The terminal observed system is the set of global sections of the presheaf of
sentence-evaluations. The translation conditions (O) are the satisfaction condition restricted
to the observed sentences. What an institution does not carry is an order on contexts that is
independent of signature inclusion, a component of authority separate from satisfaction, and
a transition function on models; the lax condition (A) and the simulation condition (D) have

                                       49

no counterpart there, and the failure of the commutation criterion of Section 4 is invisible to
an institution because navigation is not a morphism of signatures. The framework is therefore
best described as institution-like in its observational reduct and as a strict extension of it in
authority and dynamics, and a precise comparison, which would exhibit the observational
reduct of CRS as a full subcategory of a category of institutions, has not been carried out
here.

Comparison with scope graphs and coalgebraic semantics.  The scope-graph calculus
of [29] defines name resolution by reachability under a path policy, which corresponds in this
essay to the specification of the observation presheaf from a graph, and Proposition 6.5 records
that scope graphs strictly generalize scope trees. The calculus does not address the comparison
of resolution disciplines across languages, nor authority or transitions. Coalgebraic treatments
of behavioral equivalence [37] characterize the coarsest bisimulation of a transition system,
and Proposition 11.5 is the instance of this for the partial transition function used here; the
observational quotient XU differs from the behavioral quotient exactly by the distinction
illustrated in Example 13.6.

Simulation-based accounts of physical reasoning. A research program in cognitive
science proposes that intuitive physical judgment is produced by approximate probabilistic
simulation, in the manner of a game physics engine, restricted to the objects and interactions
relevant to the question posed [34]. This is an empirical hypothesis about people and is not a
consequence of anything proved here, and the mathematics of this essay offers no evidence for
or against it. A formal observation is nevertheless available. A simulator that instantiates
only the objects relevant to a query computes, for each query, an observation at a restricted
context, and the requirement that answers to related queries cohere is the coherence condition
oc = Ω(u)◦od. Whether the sets of queries and simulations in such an account form a presheaf
satisfying the separation and gluing conditions of Section 10, and whether the failure modes
of that section occur in it, are questions that the experimental literature has not posed in this
form, and they are recorded as Question E.1.
